Seven comments

From an old New England compilation. The original was in B-flat, but I’ve transcribed it to A for convenience. I wonder whether this tune, in view of its title, has any connection with WW2.

↳ Posted by fidicen on November 26th, 2002.

Perhaps I should mention that the Spitfire was a fighter aircraft that had enormous influence in WW2. There are still a few around, and they make regular flying appearances at air shows.

↳ Posted by fidicen on November 26th, 2002.

An old title, actually…

This tune shows up under the title “Spit-Fire Reel” in Ryan’s Mammoth Collection, from the 1880’s, some decades before there ever was such a thing as an airplane. The dictionary definition of “spitfire” is just “a quick-tempered or highly excitable person”

↳ Posted by rwwt on October 28th, 2010.

Lisa Ornstein’s, X:2

This is the version recorded by Gerry O’Connor in 1991; Lá Lugh, Track 14.c.

Gerry got it from Lisa Ornstein so I assume the “4 turn version” is hers whereby part 1 is played between 4 different versions of part 2 (2“A”, 2“B” & 2“E”) in a sort of strophic way not uncommon in Quebec.

Played;
1. 2A. 1. 2B. 1. 2E. 1. 2A’(var) & 1(var.) to end.
Part 1 is used as a chorus between verses and this role is ‘amplified’ by the tune being played tutti and the various turns solo. It is a very effective way of drawing people’s ear to the music.

Olivier Demers has listed a Reel Acrobate
p.191 in his 2020 Mille Airs du Québec et de l’Amérique Francophone.
Lisa Ornstein/Gerry O’Connor’s version
is based on the more common 2 part version.
The variation in B min. sounds both ‘vertically compressed’ and transposed.

↳ Posted by birlibirdie on June 30th, 2024.

Re: Reel Acrobate (Lisa Ornstein’s 4 part version)

This reel, formed out of barely 5-10 sec long, repeated and varied phrases is a compelling example of the ‘less is more’ principle;
it is fascinating to see how little original/basic/ground material is actually needed to create a fully-fledged tune (rolling at a 100mph) with ear-twisting and finger-twisting -fun- qualities to it.
Perhaps someone knows who composed the variations? Or who first recorded them?

Below: my original abc draft showing some of the “acrobatic” variations in the repeats (2nd fiddle? or dazzling technique?)
I believe the printable score is readable even though it serves to highlight / gives a flavour of what rhythmic acrobatics our dazzling northern fiddlers indulge in at terminal high speed!
